Kramat Karam (Sinar Kramat & Phang Tong Wie) and Kicir-Kicir (Jetty with an Orchestra Gambang Keromong & Suhairi): found on a 2020 Golden Century compilation of old Indonesian records, whose release dates (2020, 2013) are reissue dates, so years are null. Pang Tjin Nio's own Irama Masa cassette albums of the early 1980s (listed by name on Indonesian Wikipedia) were not found on any readable catalogue page.

Benyamin S., Funky Kromong Vol. 1 (2022, MusicBrainz 7ca00128-f008-43cd-bb28-a921f9d43e99): seen in a search only, not read, left out.

unverified: 暁に祈る (伊藤久男, film theme 1940): kept, but Japanese Wikipedia's lead calls it a 戦時歌謡 (wartime popular song); the gunka tie is only a section heading '軍歌『暁に祈る』'. The lead may prefer to drop it.

愛国行進曲 (東京音楽学校): the page calls it a national patriotic song and 'de facto second national anthem', not a gunka in so many words; the tie rests on that, on the album title (軍歌・愛国歌・戦時歌謡) and on the Columbia credit to the 東京音楽学校 on the same page.

Release years of the Columbia original-78 reissue tracks 愛国行進曲, 海ゆかば and 暁に祈る are left null: iTunes shows only the 2014 reissue or a 1955 date, and no page read dates those exact takes. 露営の歌 (1937), 燃ゆる大空 (1940) and 若鷲の歌 (1943) are dated by their Wikipedia pages naming the same singers and Columbia/Nitchiku.
ふじの山 and 朧月夜: tied only by the 文部省唱歌 page naming them among the best-known Monbushō shōka; no song page was read, so the year written is null (recalled as 1910 and 1914, not confirmed).
同期の桜: year written given as 1938, the date of Saijō Yaso's source poem 戦友の唄 in 少女倶楽部; the gunka text itself was adapted later (the page's first broadcast record is 1945).
軍艦: year written 1897 is the page's 'about 1897' (頃) for Setoguchi's setting; Toriyama's words date from 1893.

Recalled, not looked up or not reachable: 蛍の光 (1881), 春が来た, 紅葉, 村祭, 鯉のぼり (Japanese Wikipedia titles for the last three were not found by direct address and the search API refused the script with a rate limit), 元寇, 水師営の会見, 加藤隼戦闘隊, 父よあなたは強かった; all are on the albums read but have no genre tie read.
A Korean changga near-miss (e.g. 학도가, sung to the Tetsudō shōka tune) was not made: Korean Wikipedia has no page for it and no recording was read.
Nothing recorded before 1937 was verified: the earliest takes in the playlist are the Columbia 78s of 1937-43; Meiji and Taishō songs appear in post-war re-recordings with null or late release years.

Gerald Wickremesooriya's Nurthi Gee recording: named on English Wikipedia; not found on iTunes or MusicBrainz.
Shrilal Abeykoon's 1990s nurthi cassettes, Manike Attanayake and Ramya Wanigasekara (radio nurthi singers): no recording found on iTunes Sri Lanka.

Sunday Observer 2011 article (archives.sundayobserver.lk/2011/05/01/mon14.asp): the site answered with a bot check; not used.

Tracks from Historia musical del porro pelayero (2004 anthology) carry null years: the anthology date is not the recording date. Porrovia also lists María Varilla by Banda 19 de Marzo de Laguneta with 1962-01-01, not used.

María Varilla's composer Alejandro Ramírez Ayazo and Lucho Bermúdez classics as recorded by himself (Carmen de Bolívar, Salsipuedes, San Fernando, Colombia tierra querida, on MusicBrainz 'San Fernando y otros éxitos inolvidables', Sonolux 1954): no readable page labels those recordings porro, so left out; the es.wikipedia pages for María Varilla (canción) and Alejandro Ramírez Ayazo returned 404.
Pachito E'ché, Se va el caimán and Me voy pa' Cataca are named on English Wikipedia as porros that influenced 1960s bands, but no recording of them was read, so left out.
Totó la Momposina, Juan Piña, Billo's Caracas Boys, Los Melódicos, Miguel Emiro Naranjo's other bands: named on Wikipedia as porro performers, not looked up for recordings.

Historia musical del porro pelayero also holds fandangos (e.g. Fandango viejo, Banda Bajera de San Pelayo); only tracks Wikipedia names as porros (María Varilla, La mona Carolina, Roque Guzmán, Soy pelayero) or that are not otherwise labelled (Sara Esther) were used, so Sara Esther's porro tie is by album title only.
Wikipedia API search was rate-limited during this run (too many requests), so Spanish Wikipedia song articles were not searched further.

No period recording (1920s 78) of any changga was found on a page a script can read: MusicBrainz has none for 희망가, 학도가 or 사의 찬미 before 1975; iTunes Korea store search returned nothing (the US store was used). Yun Sim-deok's own 1926 사의 찬미, Chae Gyu-yeop's 학도가 and 희망가, and Park Chae-seon and Lee Ryu-saek's 1925 이 풍진 세월 are named on Wikipedia but no release page was read.

Artist names in Hangul only where a fetched page shows them (고운봉 from English Wikipedia Trot; 신카나리아, 진송남, 별셋, 김경남 from iTunes; 한영애 from MusicBrainz search). 소년행진가 by 김경남 is tied by title only to 안창호's 소년행진가 named by the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture; the album page does not credit the lyricist.
1916 Hawaii Honolulu Korean Anthem (Incheon Concert Chamber, iTunes 1668257183) holds eleven patriotic songs that look like changga, but no page tying it to a changga songbook was found; left out.
용진가 and other tracks on 독립군가 모음집 are independence-army songs (E0015973) not named as 계몽창가 in E0072538; left out.
Start date conflict: the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture 창가 entry dates 황제탄신경축가 to 1876 in its summary and to 1896 in its body; Korean Wikipedia gives 동심가 of 1896. The window uses 1896.

Year written is given only for 사의 찬미 (1926, recorded that year). 희망가 is dated 1925 ('발표') on Korean Wikipedia 한국의 가요사 but that page was not cited as a claim; 학도가 exists in several versions (1905 Kim In-sik; the Railway Song melody) and the recorded one is not identified, so both carry null.
